turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, it's a pleasure to meet you. I guess... well, to be honest, the main thing that brings me in is that since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. 

I mean, everybody tells you retirement is supposed to be relaxing, right? You sit in the recliner, watch a little TV, maybe do some fishing or just enjoy the quiet. But not me. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next, all day long, just... bang, bang, bang. It’s honestly like I still have a crew waiting on me to tell them what to do. Back when I was working, I was always on my feet, making sure things were running right, and it's like my body didn't get the memo that I don't have a timecard to punch anymore. 

I'll start out organizing the workbench in the garage, and then ten minutes later I'm out fixing a sprinkler head, and then I'm sweeping the driveway, and then I'm back in the house looking for a squeaky door hinge to oil. My wife says I'm wearing a track into the carpet. I just can't sit still for more than a couple minutes without feeling like I need to be doing something, fixing something, moving somewhere. I really thought it would wear off after I retired, you know, just give it a few months to settle in and get used to the quiet life, but it hasn't stopped at all. It's actually exhausting, to tell you the truth, just being on the go from sunup to sundown for absolutely no reason, but I just can't seem to turn the motor off.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an inability to sit still for more than a couple of minutes and a constant feeling of needing to be moving or doing something.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states he is 'on the go from sunup to sundown' and 'can't seem to turn the motor off.'

turns.doctor_question: During these times when you are constantly moving and working, do you feel an overwhelming sense of happiness, excitement, or feeling 'on top of the world'?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh no. No, nothing like that at all. I wouldn't say I'm excited, and I definitely don't feel on top of the world. Honestly, it's more of a... well, it's a nuisance, really. I'm not out there whistling a happy tune or feeling like I just won the lottery or anything. 

My wife actually asked me something similar just last week. She was watching me weed the front flower beds—which, by the way, I didn't even plan to do, I just went out to get the mail and saw a dandelion by the mailbox, and the next thing I know I'm on my hands and knees in the dirt for an hour and a half—and she came out and said, "Do you even enjoy doing all this?" And I had to stop and really think about it, and I told her, no, not really. It's not a happy feeling at all. I don't feel energized in a good way, I just feel... pushed. Like there's this hum inside me that says I have to keep going, keep fixing, keep doing. 

But I'm 65, you know? My knees aren't what they used to be back when I was running work crews. So physically, I'm just tired. I would absolutely love to feel relaxed and happy just sitting on the back porch with a glass of iced tea, like a normal retired guy. But if I try that, I just get all antsy and my mind starts listing off ten other things that need a coat of paint or a new screw. So, no, definitely no overwhelming happiness or excitement. It's just work. I'm just moving because if I don't, I feel like I can't settle anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling 'antsy' and unable to settle down.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient states they are unable to relax and sit quietly on the porch without becoming antsy.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling a 'hum inside me that says I have to keep going' and constantly moving.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies feeling an overwhelming sense of happiness, excitement, or feeling 'on top of the world'.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your life, did you experience this same level of restlessness, constant need to be doing something, or difficulty sitting still when you were much younger, like when you were in school?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my sister about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes of our parents' stuff, and she found some of my old report cards from elementary school. And... yeah, the short answer is yes, absolutely. But it wasn't just the moving around, though there was plenty of that. 

I mean, even back in grade school, I was always the kid who couldn't quite keep it together. My teachers—and I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade specifically, she was a wonderful lady but she had zero patience for me—they always said I was a bright kid, you know, smart enough to do the work, but I was just completely scattered. I'd sit down to do a math worksheet, and two minutes later I'm up sharpening my pencil, and then I'm looking out the window at a bird, and then I've lost the pencil entirely. I went through so many pencils my mother thought I was eating them. 

And I couldn't just sit there and wait my turn, either. If I knew the answer to something, I'd just blurt it right out. Bang, just like that. I didn't mean to be disrespectful, I just... the thought would pop into my head and it had to come out of my mouth right that second. Mrs. Gable was always having to remind me, "Raise your hand, raise your hand." And finishing assignments? Forget about it. They'd always have to remind me to finish my work before I could go out for recess, because I'd get halfway through and just drift off onto something else. So, yeah, that feeling of being driven, of being scattered and not being able to just sit still and focus... that's been with me pretty much my whole life, as far back as I can remember. It just looked a little different back then, I guess, because I was a kid in a classroom instead of an old man in a garage.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes getting halfway through assignments and drifting off, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions needing constant reminders from teachers to finish their schoolwork before recess.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports constantly losing pencils during school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as looking out the window at a bird.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient notes getting up from their seat shortly after sitting down to do a worksheet.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms a lifelong inability to just sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly mentions a 'feeling of being driven', which aligns with acting as if driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits to blurting out answers before being called on.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states they could not sit and wait their turn.
